tagline: Paste text and get a readability grade, plus highlighted long sentences, adverbs, and passive voice.
verdictSummary: The actual Hemingway feature set — a Flesch-Kincaid-style grade-level score, and rule-based highlighting of long sentences, adverbs, and passive constructions — is entirely deterministic and genuinely a one-sitting build, no model required for the core loop. Adding an optional LLM rewrite button on top is a clean extra, not a dependency; the deterministic scoring is what actually earns the "yes."
coreLoopDIY: Paste or type text into an editor, compute a readability grade level and highlight long sentences, adverbs, passive-voice constructions, and complex words in real time with no network call, and optionally send a highlighted sentence to an LLM for a rewrite suggestion.
whatYouLose: years of tuning on exactly which sentence patterns actually read as awkward, not just technically long
cross-device sync of documents and settings
team style guides shared across an organization
polish on the AI rewrite feature specifically, versus a generic prompt
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for Hemingway because a deterministic readability score is easy to compute but hard to tune — flagging genuinely awkward sentences without also flagging every technically-long-but-clear one takes real editorial calibration across a lot of real writing, which is exactly the kind of tuning a first-pass local build won't have out of the box.
prompt:
Build a local readability editor: deterministic grade-level scoring and highlighting, with an optional LLM rewrite. Stack: a local web app (React + a small Node backend, or fully client-side), no database required — this operates on whatever text is pasted in, session by session.

Core loop: as the user types or pastes text, compute a Flesch-Kincaid grade-level score in real time using a standard, well-documented formula (syllables per word, words per sentence) — entirely client-side, no network call. Highlight, with distinct colors: sentences over roughly 20 words ("hard to read"), adverbs (via a simple suffix/word-list heuristic, not a full NLP model), passive-voice constructions (a regex-based heuristic looking for "was/were + past participle" patterns), and complex words that have simpler common alternatives (matched against a small hand-built substitution list). Clicking a flagged sentence optionally sends just that sentence to an LLM API for a rewrite suggestion, shown as an accept-or-reject diff — this part is opt-in and the app is fully useful without it.

The deterministic scoring needs no API key at all. The optional rewrite feature needs an Anthropic or OpenAI key; without one, that button is simply hidden or disabled, and the core scoring and highlighting work exactly the same.

Do not build: cross-device sync, browser or Google Docs extensions, or team style-guide sharing — this is a single-document local editor. Do not let the passive-voice or adverb heuristics silently over-flag; document their known false-positive patterns in the README rather than pretending the regex is a full grammar model.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Hemingway documents?
faq.a: Hemingway doesn't store documents server-side by default — most users' text lives wherever they wrote it originally, so there's nothing to migrate beyond copy-pasting into the new editor.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: As a responsive web page, the scoring and highlighting work on mobile, though editing longer text comfortably is still better suited to a keyboard.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing for the core scoring and highlighting — it's pure local computation. The optional LLM rewrite costs a fraction of a cent per sentence sent, only when you click it.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Calibration. Hemingway's rules were tuned over years against real writing to catch genuinely awkward sentences without flooding the page with false positives; a first-pass regex heuristic here will both miss real problems and over-flag clear, simply long sentences until you spend real time tuning it against your own writing.
